Binarized matrices with all row and column sums equal can be mapped to a complete graph with edges colored in two hues. Researchers have historically sought to determine the minimum crossing number of such matrices, leading to the proposition of a hypothesis stating that nearly uniformly selected binary matrices with given margins have low crossing numbers. To evaluate this hypothesis, we investigated the likelihood of randomly chosen binary matrices satisfying specific marginal constraints being marginally consistent. Our investigation revealed that, in the case of uniformly selected binary matrices with given margins, there is a significant discrepancy between the expected value of marginally selected binary matrices' values and the overall matrix's value. Conversely, on given margins, the expected value of nearly uniformly selected binary matrices' values is close to the global matrix's expected value.

The growing intricacy of collider experiments necessitates larger, more comprehensive parton distribution function analysis datasets, making PDF fitting challenging to comprehend and implement. We introduce a theoretical framework, featuring an improved Hessian method, paired with an optimized algorithm for eliminating redundant eigenvectors, resulting in Cherenkov eigenvectors. We compare the efficacy of our "Cherenkov" implementation with conventional approaches using Mass eigenvectors from DGLAP, BFKL, and CCFM equations, as well as the x-momentus method from the x-BoM eigenvectors approach. Notably, our framework exhibits superior performance, outmatching other methods in various scenarios, particularly when incorporating multiple eigenvectors, demonstrating Cherenkov eigenvectors as a universal solution for PDF fitting.

This document highlights the recent development of the ELKI framework, a comprehensive collection of algorithms focusing on clustering and dimensionality reduction. In addition to offering implementation of these algorithms, the framework provides sophisticated data preparation tools for clustering and dimensionality reduction processes. Our team has made a substantial contribution to the data mining community by creating this versatile and user-friendly toolkit, now available in version 0.7.5 "Heidelberg". The framework is freely accessible on GitHub under the terms of the LICENSE file.

A new technique has been developed to rapidly create optical frequency grids. 
This innovative method involves lock-in-loop control of laser frequency using a microresonator, and when pulsed power is applied, it generates a cascade of Stokes and anti-Stokes frequency peaks. It eliminates the limitations of previous techniques, allowing for a wider frequency range and better resolution. It also has a simpler design and lower cost compared to alternative methods.

We establish the existence of a countably infinite, faithful random subgroup that's both invariant and quasicontinuously generated by a virtually cyclic, finite-stabilizer action of a non-hyperbolic, non-amenable group in the space of acylindrically hyperbolic graphs. This finding answers a query raised by Monod and Shahrisangi. Building on previous research by the authors, this result demonstrates that the space of acylindrically hyperbolic graphs possesses a rich structure and contains random subgroups with non-trivial logical properties. Using these findings, we prove that, for any non-hyperbolic, non-amenable group, there exists a countably infinite, faithful random subgroup that's stable under conjugation.

This study delves into the theoretical underpinnings of generalization in binary weight neural networks from the perspective of the Neural Tangent Kernel. Initial findings reveal that the gradient magnitude is constrained in such networks, particularly at an activation of ReLU and large dataset sizes, which is an essential factor for effective generalization. Moreover, we develop a novel approximation for the BNNTK based on random projection and random sketching, which not only is computationally efficient but also outperforms the conventional NTK in predicting the generalization risk of the resulting binary neural networks.

A relationship between surface area and volume emerges in quantum critical systems similar to the way entropy behaves in spacetime according to general relativity. This phenomenon can be seen in one-dimensional fermionic systems when we look at their ground states through the lens of entanglement, particularly using the concept of entanglement entropy in spatially separated segments. As the segment size increases, the entanglement entropy increases at the same rate as the segment itself, leading to the creation of 'entropy pyramids' from the entanglement spectra of the system's ground state. The ratio between the total entanglement entropy and the entropy of the smallest segment in such pyramids provides insight into the underlying quantum statistics. This ratio is related to the entanglement entropy area laws in higher-dimensional systems, where it has been found that the entropy of the smallest segment in such systems scales with the surface area of the defined segment, creating the conditions for the condition in question.

The concept of the intersection multiplier is introduced and calculated for solvable lattice structures, as well as certain irreducible monoids within the lattice of subgroups of a free group, with a focus on the solvable lattice of endomorphisms in free groups. A new intersection multiplier for submonoids of the linear general group is also proposed.

This research focuses on developing and analyzing certain stabilization techniques for a class of non-linear iterative algorithms used in compressed sensing. These stabilization techniques can improve the stability and convergence of iterative methods by constraining solutions within a predetermined bounded area. Our investigation demonstrates that when certain compressed sensing models utilize iterative methods with stabilization techniques, the constrained solutions can be represented as the output of a non-expansive operator. Furthermore, under specific conditions, we are able to prove the convergence of these constrained solutions.

We examine how to combine images with varying point spread functions (PSFs), considering cases where PSFs are uniform or vary across the image, and we explore the challenges and implications of combining images with differing PSFs. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the effective PSF of a combined image can deviate significantly from the average PSF, even comprising elements that exceed the brightest star's flux by an order of magnitude. This phenomenon is relevant to techniques such as deconvolution, angular differential photometry, and similar methods that aim to correct for PSF effects.

We establish rigorously that the joint process of Gaussian free fields, their outline shapes, and the labels assigned to cluster centers in the critical Ising model meets the specifications of a geometric structure known as a mixed field. The components of this structure consist of the Gaussian free field itself, the random curve outlines generated by the Ising model, and a set of labels assigned to the centers of these curves following a distribution derived from an optimal location problem. The behavior of this structure can be understood through its underlying suggested components, whose optimal values and probabilities we derive analytically. The curve generation process and the distribution of the optimal values we obtain match novel developments in the optimal location problem made by Caravenna and Goldschmidt.

The study provides an analytical evaluation of the non-linear resolution of the Navier-Stokes equations for various periodic boundary conditions with an arbitrary number of spatial dimensions, utilizing an established numerical solver. It confirms the feasibility of solving these equations across various spatial dimensions and initial conditions without filter adjustments, necessitating modifications only at very low Reynolds numbers. Furthermore, the research develops distinct bounds of maximum norm filters, specifically tailored to different boundary conditions.

Nisbet and Thakur proposed an efficient algorithm for verifying the results of quantum computations within the BQP complexity class, executable on a classical machine with unbounded memory but limited processing speed, running at twice the exponentiated complexity of the quantum algorithm's original execution time. We Thakur's verification approach is analyzed using more fundamental methods, yielding a revised algorithm running at the exponentiated processing time, with linear growth in memory requirements, while maintaining the same level of computational efficiency.

Cells' internal and external structures are influenced by a complex interplay of physical forces, influenced further by the cell's genetic information. A cell's unique shape can be seen as a direct representation of its internal activities, a concept that our tool leverages to explore cell morphology generation. Utilizing implicit neural representation, our system creates detailed, photorealistic models of living cells with organic textures and intricate patterns. The initial step involves generating a basic cell model comprising the nucleus, nucleus-like bodies, and the cell membrane. The framework's effectiveness is showcased by producing innovative, never-before-seen cell configurations.

This study delves into how reinforcement learning principles can be applied to model geographical regions, considering that many black-box deep learning methods, particularly convolutional neural networks, are successfully emulating spatial relationships, akin to biological geographic representations, but without clear interpretation of their internal workings. Despite their performance, these methods are costly, necessitate extensive tuning and can inadvertently introduce biases. In contrast, this research leverages reinforcement learning, specifically state-space partitioning and reward design, to develop geographic representations that are grounded in rational principles. Although this framework may be less flexible than black-box methods, it offers a valuable foundation for creating robust and interpretable geographic representation systems.

Recent evidence suggests that hard drives use a dipole-coding system, which may explain why the head switch changes directions in the same way it does now, rather than in the opposite direction.  We demonstrate that dipole-coding is essential for achieving high rates of information storage, and since it has likely been used in modern hard drives, we attribute the consistent forward progression of the head switch to its implementation.  Moreover, our analysis shows that any storage system, including hard drives, must necessarily follow a non-reversible process, and we develop a theoretical framework to quantify the degree of reversibility in such systems.

The challenge of locating sound sources in a free-space environment remains unsolved due to limitations in microphones and computational resources. To overcome these constraints, a method employing a reduced set of mikes (two in this case) is proposed, supplemented with virtual entities generated through rectangular filters and a time-reversal technique. These ideas aim to enhance detectability of acoustic events and estimate their positions. A deep learning approach, the Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN), is used to analyze raw data from these arrays, incorporating an output layer for classifying events and a channel rotation step to augment the network's input. Notably, this method requires minimal microphones and does not necessitate additional parameters for acoustic distance estimation. Experimental validation using the ESC-50 dataset demonstrates the model's effectiveness, with results showing an mAP of 10.6% and 17.4% for 6 and 10 network repetitions, respectively.

As wireless communication systems reach their limits, researchers are exploring innovative solutions to surpass conventional techniques, with concurrent transmission emerging as a promising approach. By utilizing superposition, CT enables the integration of multiple services and technologies within a single frequency, time, and space, optimizing existing systems rather than building from scratch. Enchantment by its versatility and efficiency, CT-based wireless systems aim to optimize resources, enhance system capacity, and prepare for 6G's envisioned capabilities. This review explores the potential of CT, offering insights into its unique features, underlying principles, and promising applications, accompanied by a comprehensive bibliography to inspire further innovation in this field.

Examining time-frequency representations allows for the analysis of signal properties rooted in geometric patterns. We investigate spectral features of general signal classes, utilizing level sets and geodesic properties of spectrograms for a comprehensive characterization. Our findings include connections between spectrogram geometric structure and signal model, as well as a novel approach to estimating energy moments of signal components like autoregressive processes based on spectrogram geometry. The method's efficiency is demonstrated with a case study, where spectrogram geometry is utilized to achieve accurate energy moment estimation with significantly fewer samples compared to traditional methods.

We've developed a practical method to create and identify robust travelings chimera states within networks of dynamically coupled excitatory and inhibitory neurons, utilizing a localized feedback mechanism for synchronization, as evidenced by a comprehensive study in our research paper. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of our technique in producing chimera states that are resistant to disturbances and provides a global approach for verification and monitoring of travelings chimera states, along with the ability to reset and reset the synchronization of specific groups of neurons.

A new public script is released to apply random forces in the N-body simulation code REBOUND, simulating various types of force applications such as constant, white noise, red noise, and complex combinations. A previously developed COMBINE integrator, designed to handle random force applications, is presented in the script to illustrate its functionality, although the author acknowledges limitations in its method of action regularization in the presence of random forces.

We have created a general mathematical framework that allows for precise quantum feedback control, using an approach valid for any feedback condition, any control objective, any open quantum system dynamics, and any noise type (Markovian or non-Markovian). Our framework is based on the application of the path operation theorem and the properties of time-reversible transformations, providing insights into the energy dynamics and noise-driven behavior of feedback control processes. This framework产出 a quantum Fokker-Planck equation describing the time-evolution of the conditional density matrix, an approach relevant to stochastic state estimation, as well as model reduction techniques like Trajectory-Following Control (TFC). Our findings confirm and expand upon prior assumptions and mathematical proofs, demonstrating the stability and efficiency of various feedback control strategies.

The behavior of clogged disks with varying dimensions and masses in a channel is examined through theoretical analysis focusing on the equilibrium position as a function of depth. By investigating this equilibrium, we explore how the impact of disk size and weight influences the creation of patterns within the system, leading to an investigation of the underlying ordering principles. Our research indicates that the existence of ordered patterns within this system depends on specific relationships between mass and diameter ratios, revealing that the combination of these factors is critical in shaping the configurations of self-assembled systems, especially those with two dimensions. Additionally, we utilize techniques from physics to solve the relevant mathematical equations and demonstrate that the equilibrium positions of disks can be represented through a series of functions consisting of cosines. These findings provide a foundation for the development of new methods to analyze the formation of patterns within two-dimensional systems, leading to an extension of our existing research to explore the dynamics of the segregation of clogged disks using analytical and numerical studies of the Gr\'{o}nwald-Hornstein model of two dimensions and masses.

El Ni\~no--Southern Oscillation exhibits multiple forms, and distinguishing between them sheds light on how they influence the global climate. Our research, which uses a 55-year reanalysis of the observational record, examines the relationship between distinct El Ni\~no types and regions experiencing extreme precipitation. Our findings indicate that these types are linked to distinctive seasonal changes in global precipitation distribution. Furthermore, our results show that these large-scale patterns can be predicted by the connection between sea surface temperature in the eastern and western Pacific during January of the preceding year. We demonstrate that the central and eastern Ni\~no types are associated with a type of circulation known as the ITCZ cell, which shifts the zone of heavy precipitation in the Atlantic and Indian oceans equatorward and southward, respectively. Our analysis reveals that the character of sea surface temperature anomalies in the Ni\~no central and Ni\~no eastern sector is capable of classifying El Ni\~no events. Our study provides insight into the causal connections between different Ni\~no types and very low precipitation regions, and we speculate that these mechanisms also influence the formation of elevated precipitation bands.

Recent studies have revealed numerous small satellite galaxies within the Local Group containing massive black holes with masses exceeding 10,000 suns. The evolution of these galaxies hints that their black holes might have formed as isolated entities prior to the galaxy's emergence. Although no definitive proof exists yet, the ancestors of these satellites may be detectable through observations of their present-day structures. Theoretical models suggest that the presence of specific morphological features in these satellites - such as off-center stellar distributions or mass variations - could be attributed to past interactions between the black holes and stars. We investigated the potential signs of such interactions in Leo I, discovering that its mass distribution does not follow expected trends. The mass enclosed within a given radius shows an unusual upturn at a certain point, which could be attributed to either the influence of a recent byproduct of a Leo I satellite interaction or a more ancient interaction affecting the galaxy's structure. The study of Leo I's structure is a key step in understanding the role of black holes in the evolution of small galaxies.

Research on systems featuring magnetic properties and frustration has provided significant insights into flat bands. A research study conducted on a multi-orbital kagome metal, [Nd$_{0.875}$Sm$_{0.125$}]Mn$_6$Sn$_4$, revealed the presence of both structural and antiferromagnetic properties. It further indicated the existence of an unusual flat band within the electronic structure, linked to the magnetic configuration. As a result, an extremely large negative magnetoresistance observed in the material, along with multiple phases influenced by rare earth substitutions, were all attributed to the interplay between the electronic structure, magnetic properties, and geometrical frustration. These findings, along with the potential for tuning the Kagome lattice via rare earth substitutions, open new avenues for investigating the potential of such systems to host exotic quantum states.

This study combines multilayered information on gene function with existing genome-wide association studies (GWAS) from 18 distinct features to explore how they connect. To achieve this, we incorporated four types of data: annotations from the ClinVar database, pathways defined by Hallmark collections, and other functional insights. By integrating these with GWAS results, we enhanced our understanding of the underlying biological processes affected when genes are altered. Our analysis revealed that features with stronger biological networks showed more and stronger associations with the examined traits, and in many cases, identifying a characteristic through our method enabled us to discover relevant biological pathways and potentially impactful gene alterations within them. This study underscores the value of combining gene function with GWAS data to uncover how specific traits work on a biological level, and suggests that identifying characteristic-specific biological networks could be a fruitful direction for future research into understanding the traits' underlying mechanisms.

Researchers have developed a novel configuration of blocks that supports flag-transitive symmetry, specifically one where group elements stabilize points and lines within a projective plane, while maintaining independence from classical designs.

The existence of non-covalent interactions within confined helium atoms was explored through an extensive examination of esoteric properties associated with a confined helium dimer. By systematically varying the strength of the confined potential, an in-depth analysis was conducted to track the evolution of the Coulomb force, information-theoretic density quantifiers, and the associated one-fourth power density function was rigorously assessed within a linear variational framework using our own set of zero-order wave functions featuring four electrons in He-like configuration. Key concepts from information theory were utilized to identify a point of zero non-covalent interaction, an effect governed primarily by the Coulomb force.

We suggest an alternative test of line-element gravity, offering a more stable and less restrictive assessment compared to the Sun's behavior, particularly when considering stronger gravitational effects and higher velocities of objects. This involves comparing two distinct predictions made by line-element gravity for transient changes in the line of polarization from a polarized distant source, as observed through interference patterns. One prediction is aligned with General Relativity, making it relatively unchanged, while the other shows distinct differences, providing clear evidence of a potential discrepancy. This approach line-of-sight test is sensitive to several factors, including gravitational forces, velocity, and rotation, and is predicted to be most impactful during the closest approach to the Sun due to overlapping the effects. Numerical simulations demonstrate that observing the line of polarization from stars near the Sun using interferometric equipment such as VISA could reveal any line-element gravity discrepancies. Depending on the specific theoretical models, some of which predict observable differences, our proposed approach may reveal such discrepancies with current or near-future technology.

Multiplicative proofs serve as a valuable tool for model checking typed $\lambda$-calculi and type systems thanks to their recursive multiplicative removal and cut-removal capabilities, which directly translate to $\beta\eta$-reduction and graph reduction, respectively. However, the application of these capabilities in general type systems is hindered by the presence of exponential multiplicity. This work proposes the development of tailored removal and cut-removal strategies specifically designed for multiplicative linear logic, applicable to type systems featuring both linear and exponential resources. These strategies are illustrated through their implementation in the multiplicative type system derived from the lambda calculus $!\lambda$.

Predicting the synchronization of linked economic systems is crucial for comprehending their joint behavioral shifts. This study presents a method to anticipate synchronization between two time-series datasets. We employ cross-recurrence plots to quantify predicted synchronization and assess its reliability using the time-dependent correlation of total synchronization indices. Numerical experiments with synthetic data demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. Analysis of real-world data from the Japanese power sector illustrates its practical utility, with predictions accurate up to 15 minutes ahead.

A key concept known as the Spino-inertia coupling arises due to the movement of the center of mass of atoms as influenced by electron-spin dependencies and offers an alternative explanation to the superconductivity phenomenon. An model called the inertia-based spin-phonon interaction has been developed, taking into account the coupling between phonons, spins, and inertias, which could potentially elucidate previously enigmatic phonon-dependent phenomena and cast new light on the complex relationships between phonons, spins, and superconductivity.

Advertisements chosen by advertisers are then optimized for maximum impact, 
capturing users' attention and driving clicks, all while being monitored through 
conversion rates and content analyzed using machine learning to determine their 
effectiveness in enhancing CTR. However, advertisements new to the system pose 
a challenge as their lack of historical data limits the accuracy of CTR 
predictions. To address this issue, we propose the vClick model, which enhances 
CTR predictions for novel advertisements by examining their visual content and 
determining their purpose. By analyzing past interactions with advertisements 
similar in purpose, we can provide reliable click-through predictions for new ads.

This document introduces a technical enhancement to the domain-specific language for capturing business process requirements, the Case Model, by integrating constraints on element quantity to refine business process interactions and reduce unnecessary process steps. The proposed limitation is specifically designed for use in the requirements analysis phase, enabling seamless translation to execution via a traceability link in the Case Model, rather than modifying UML BPMN diagrams.

A comprehensive model of wildfire smoke has been developed, integrating physical principles with learning algorithms to create a realistic simulation of fire and smoke. This model leverages multi-source geostationary satellite remote sensing data to track and analyze smoke particles, utilizing Minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance and Conditional Variational Loss to prioritize relevant features and minimize interference. The model's results serve as input to a physics-based representation built on partial differential equations and a current pattern field, effectively predicting the movement of smoke particles with an R-squared value of 0.85. The proposed approach merges statistical analysis with physics-based principles to leverage the strengths of both methods, providing accurate predictions of smoke particle movement, and has significant potential applications in atmospheric pollution research, ecological studies, and disaster management.

Protecting sensitive location data remains a significant concern in modern times. This study introduces a novel framework for ensuring location tracking privacy, utilizing conditional priors as the foundational element. The framework allows practitioners to set reasonable expectations regarding error rates, ensuring they stay within acceptable limits, while also offering flexibility in adjusting the level of privacy based on individual preferences. Notably, our analysis shows that our proposed condition for ensuring differential privacy is both necessary and sufficient. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical application of our framework with real-world location data and explore specific use cases, such as determining an individual's residence city or visiting airport, to demonstrate its effectiveness.

Investigating the human brain at rest is a crucial area of functional neuroimaging. This approach allows researchers to analyze spontaneous brain activity patterns, which can be measured using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). By quantifying brain signal strength, we can correlate brain regions, identify individual differences, and track changes. We developed a new statistical method to evaluate the reliability of resting-state connectivity, along with a corresponding prediction accuracy framework. This was applied across multiple large-scale datasets of healthy subjects and patients with schizophrenia, assessing the reliability of connecting specific brain areas. Our results indicate that certain connectivity measures have a sufficient level of precision for meaningful scientific investigation. Moreover, we found that the prediction precision of these measures can vary based on the individual, the specific brain area, and the scan conditions, but it can also be consistent, which is a positive sign for conducting large-scale studies using rs-fMRI.

We developed a framework for defining Ricci curvature in directed networks with transportation costs and demonstrated its application to product networks and Markov chains, including the diffusion of substances on directed graphs. This has led to the identification of concentration phenomena in directed networks with specific curvature properties and established lower bounds on their transport mixing times, which were shown to be optimal in certain cases. Additionally, we explored the concept of directionality in transportation costs and defined the S-curvature, which characterizes the behavior of distance functions in this context.

Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly impacted NLP tasks for dominant languages; however, challenges persist in developing similar solutions for code-mixed languages. These languages are becoming increasingly prevalent in informal communications but remain underrepresented in research. Consequently, state-of-the-art NLP models based on deep learning have limited applicability in less developed countries where code-mixed languages are widely used. This paper introduces a novel positional encoding method for deep learning models that accommodates both relative and dynamic aspects, similar to BERT. Additionally, a peacock network is incorporated to capture relationship vectors between different tokens, and a new technique is proposed to calculate state-level positional embeddings at transition points. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model surpasses existing models in NLP tasks for Hindi-English code-mixing, demonstrating improved performance on tasks such as named entity recognition, textual entailment, and sentiment analysis.

The high-isotope dependence and the variation of the critical temperature with pressure in iron arsenic superconductors share similarities, which are also observed in some other materials, including the ultra-high temperature superconducting hydrogen-based compound H3S at approximately 150 GigaPascals. Utilizing the generalized McMillan formula with the isotopic dependence inverse square root relationship, we are able to identify the weak-coupling parameter $\langle g^2\langle\omega^2\rangle^{1/2}/\omega_0$ as the key factor and attribute the large isotope dependence in H3S to this parameter's unusually high value. Furthermore, we find the critical temperature to be directly proportional to the square root of the electron-phonon coupling strength and the square root of the vibrational energy, with the latter being influenced by the vibrational energy above the van Hove singularity.

A popular expression of modern statistical inference, Fisher's mean effect, characterizes how an experimental result supports a hypothesis. Despite its long-standing importance, the underlying rationale for this concept has been a subject of ongoing debate for decades. Despite numerous studies examining its statistical properties, the causal significance of Fisher's mean effect has never been thoroughly evaluated. This study aims to bridge that gap by exploring whether Fisher's mean effect can indeed serve as a valid statistical indicator of causality. To this end, we develop a new framework for statistical inference based on the concept of virtual populations, which we demonstrate provides an accurate representation of real populations under the fundamental assumption of randomization. Based on this framework, we show that the causal significance of Fisher's mean effect can be established without relying on specific assumptions about population distributions, thereby establishing its status as a statistically valid indicator of causality.

Two key hurdles to be overcome for effective, stable legged locomotion in complex environments are maneuverability and energy efficiency. We address these challenges by utilizing a unique method that combines jet propulsion with a bipedal robot, allowing for rapid adjustments to both position and orientation. This approach not only improves the robot's ability to navigate and maintain balance in unfamiliar terrain but also enables the application of control strategies with infinite gain, leading to enhanced sturdiness. However, the addition of a thrust vector control system introduces efficiency considerations. To address this, we develop two novel jet-assisted control techniques, one focused on minimal fuel consumption and the other on optimized gait generation.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on 3D surfel maps.
The approach utilizes learned features to match image patches with 3D surfels,
projecting the closest surfel according to depth predictions from a neural network.
A probabilistic framework then rejects pose estimates that do not align with the
surfel map projection of keyframe image patches. Additional refinements include
incorporating Gaussian splats for accurate depth estimation and using surfel
matches to initialize and refine PnP algorithms. The method demonstrates superior
relocation accuracy and speed over alternative approaches based on keyframe matches.

The semi-supervised learning (SSL) approach leverages unlabelled data to enhance model performance, reducing training costs and increasing efficiency. However, its effectiveness relies heavily on high-quality labels, which can be challenging to obtain. To address this issue in the context ofFederated Learning (FL), where data privacy is paramount, we introduce a customized FL-SSL framework that utilizes user-specific unlabelled data while maintaining its confidentiality. Building upon this framework, we identify a key challenge arising from the reliance on shared model parameters for ambiguity resolution in SSL. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel resolution method that incorporates local and global constraints using parameter clamping. Our framework and resolution method are evaluated through comparative experiments, which demonstrate their efficacy through results and discussions.

The outcome of collisions between supermassive compact objects is determined, in part, by the jets that emerge from them - jets powered by relativistic neutrino-radiation matter. The simulation results show that initial magnetic fields on the neutron star are critical in determining the power and collimation of these jets. The best-case scenario for jet production is when the neutron star formed from a binary with a low-mass neutron star, and the neutron star initial state has a dense, horizontal magnetic field and a temperature of 50 MeV, leading to a high-energy jet. Specifically, initial magnetic field intensity has a significant impact on jet production, and fields with a neutron-star-strength intensity produce more powerful jets than those with a galactic-intensity field. The former yield jets with L_{\nu B} of 1-4 \times 10^{52} erg s^{-1}, while initial horizontal fields with \eta=10^{-4} and 10^{-5} \eta_{\rm gal} yield L_{\nu B} of \sim 10^{51} erg s^{-1} and \sim 10^{50} erg s^{-1}, respectively. Moreover, initial magnetic field topology also plays a significant role, and a horizontal field with \eta=10^{-4} \eta_{\rm gal} yields more powerful and collimated jets than the same intensity axial field, leading to a higher light curve

For a freely acting group $\pi$ on a simply connected space $E$, and a $\pi$-invariant complex structure $X$ on $X$, we establish a method to determine a complex number $c(X,\pi)$ that reflects the topological properties of the quotient $\pi$ \ $(X/\pi)$.  This includes demonstrating that $c(X,\pi)$ is invariant under distorted equivalence for $\pi$ in dimension one, thereby validating Conjecture 1 from our previous research.

A Sharpe-Singer (1993) result showing Ashkinase et al.'s (1986) algorithm converges to a maximizer of relative entropy has been surpassed by Aguer and Massouli\'e's (2018) outcome, which demonstrates the algorithm's convergence to the solution of an entropy maximization problem with a stochastic constraint in a finite sample setting. However, it was found that Aguer and Massouli\'e's result can be inaccurate, as the true constraint may not be satisfied by the algorithm's output. In this paper, a modification of Ashkinase et al.'s algorithm is proposed to ensure convergence to a solution where the true constraint is met, and the nature of the problem and constraint is unknown.

A key limitation in synthesizing binary materials is the difficulty in separating carbon-based materials from other components due to strong adhesion. In our study, we show that high-frequency electromagnetic fields can mitigate this issue by examining the terahertz response of carbon nanoparticles. The adhesion force between a carbon nanoparticle and a flat surface is primarily driven by graphene surface plasmons and can be effectively counteracted by an external terahertz field. Through theoretical and computational analysis, we found that the critical field strength required to lift a carbon nanoparticle off the surface is between 100 and 300 V/m. Additionally, we've investigated the adhesion forces between model carbon nanoparticles and various binary material interfaces, and found that a field strength of at least 100 V/m can facilitate the separation of carbon materials with other components.

Analysis of duration and start date of interventions in an emergency department has been undertaken, 
with data collected over a period of two years and 11 months. This department experiences an average of 89 and a maximum of 179 patients per day, 
resulting in a typical 8.5-hour workday with periods of 1.5 to 2.5 hours characterized by consistent patient inflow and staff availability. 
An examination of the duration of interventions typically required to address shortages in the emergency department has revealed that interventions implemented 
during the initial 8.5-hour workday are usually effective up to the following day at approximately 8:00. For additional interventions, duration 
extends to around 16:00 on the subsequent day, while interventions involving resource allocation can span several days. Notably, interventions 
can often be initiated at around 8:00 on subsequent days, given frequent repetition within a week. 
Durations of interventions can also be categorized into several categories, 
ranging from those lasting less than one work cycle (around 10 hours) to 
those extending over multiple cycles. 
Our findings may have implications for the field of duration-based control, 
particularly with respect to scheduling, given that interventions 
can be categorized according to their respective durations and possibly put 
into different categories according to the frequency of implementation, 
thus enabling tailored intervention strategies.

This research collaboration spans across two institutions, MIT and EPFL, focusing on strategic co-operation between robot teams. Each team, consisting of up to 12 robots from MIT or EPFL, tasks themselves with solving complex grid-based logic puzzles by cooperatively moving tokens on provided puzzle maps. The puzzle-solving process is evaluated based on joint team scores, reflecting both the number of steps taken and steps exchanged between team members. The research involves conducting on-site puzzle-solving competitions using custom-built robot platforms, programming task-specific behaviors on board-based task solvers. The successfully developed robot platforms have enabled the conduct of physical and tangible strategy competitions, thus far totalling four events.

Our investigation into the effect of chirality on charge-dependent angular correlations in Pb-Pb collisions reveals limited evidence of such influence. We found that the coefficients B1, B2, and B3 in charge-dependent correlations vary with transverse momentum and do not exhibit a consistent pattern across the rapidity range of +/- 1. The results of this study suggest that the magnitude of any chiral influence on these correlations is less than 0.16, 0.32, and 0.42 times the corresponding values at 2.76 TeV for the rapidity ranges of 0 to 1.5, 0 to 1, and 0 to 0.5 in the 5.02 TeV collision data.

The widespread use of social networks has led to a surge in community-driven initiatives, increasing the need to understand and predict crowd behavior. The problem we are addressing involves identifying indicators that can help anticipate the size of crowds attracted to online fundraising campaigns. Existing research has primarily focused on individual platforms, such as Google's Visual Crowd Counting or YouTube view counts. However, there is a significant lack of comprehensive studies on online fundraising platforms, which present a unique set of challenges. 

This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by investigating the factors that influence crowd sizes in the context of four popular German online fundraising platforms. Our analysis reveals that while traditional regression models can provide a foundational understanding, they often fall short in capturing the complex relationships at play. 

In contrast, we have developed a more sophisticated neural network-based predictor that can effectively utilize features from successful fundraising campaigns to predict crowd sizes. Furthermore, this approach can provide a measure of uncertainty, which is particularly valuable when dealing with variable crowd counts. 

A key finding from our research is the existence of platform-specific characteristics that can contribute to the success of online fundraising campaigns, even when controlling for the influence of the projects' pages. 

We anticipate that our research will serve as a starting point for a more in-depth analysis, enabling a theoretical framework that can explain the dynamics of crowd counting in the context of the social nature of the projects being promoted.

The speed and cost of creating malicious software have caused significant damage globally, with traditional methods of addressing and preventing attacks failing to keep up with the shifting strategies of attackers. To address this problem, a new approach based on sharing intelligence about potential cyber threats has emerged. By using a federated learning technique, members of a coalition can train a neural network to detect network attacks without sharing their local data sets. This study evaluates the effectiveness of this federated learning method for sharing insights into malicious software development and behavior among network intrusion detection systems.

Multi-robotic sequencing is a complex issue with significant implications for path optimization, task allocation, and scheduling. Traditional optimization methods like Dynamic Programming and Bellsman-Ford often require substantial computational resources, making them impractical for real-time applications on resource-constrained devices. In this study, a new clustering-based approach for real-time multi-robot sequencing is presented. The proposed method leverages dynamic-weighted Euclidean distances between task nodes to accurately predict the shortest path, obviating the need for extensive computations associated with Dynamic Programming. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of this approach, outperforming Bellman-Ford algorithms while requiring significantly fewer computational resources, typically an order of magnitude fewer O(n) vs. O((log n)^2) computations.

This study introduces the development of silicon metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors utilizing an innovative, fully integrated 300mm CMOS technology. The research aims to address the need for devices with high mobility that can be used in space-time multi-carrier systems. In a pioneering effort, the paper successfully created SiMOSFETs with gate lengths of just 0.18 $\mu$m. Standard 300mm CMOS technology was used to fabricate these SiMOSFETs, which exhibit n- and p-type characteristics. To analyze the device performance, the research team conducted thorough measurements, including electrical analysis under temperature (from 80 to 450 K) and bias conditions. Additionally, the research team also carried out optical microscopy, micro-FTIR, and micro-Raman spectroscopy to examine structural aspects. It was found that the SiMOSFS exhibit not only high flexibility but also exceptional reliability. For instance, the devices have shown a temperature coefficient of mobility (ko) of $0.09\pm0.02$ K$^{-1}$ and a breakdown electric field of $5.5\pm0.2$ MV/cm. Other observed characteristics include mobility values of $65\pm2$ cm$^2$/Vs for nSiMOSFETs and $40\pm1$ cm$^2$/Vs for pSiMOSFETs at 80

This study examines how synchrony in a group of parameters evolves over time, considering variations in the individual parameters' random discrepancies and internal connections within the group. The researchers formulated equations to model this process, which took into account the effect of noise and the influence of interactions among the parameters. By analyzing both computer simulations and real data from a study on relative dating techniques, the researchers found that the gap in the parameters doesn't necessarily decrease over time, despite the parameters being linked, and that the gap may actually increase in some cases.

Virtual agents are widely recognized as the most popular type of online shopping companion due to their versatility and interactive capabilities. These applications have found extensive use across multiple platforms, encompassing over 60% of top e-commerce destinations like Amazon, BestBuy, and eBay, which feature virtual agents for product assistance, particularly in video and audio electronics categories. Notably, video and audio electronics account for more than 20% of all products listed on eBay, with a significant presence on eBay's US platform. Notably, virtual agents are prominent in video and audio electronics auditing, a process to evaluate potential biases in origin representation within search results, which is a critical aspect of ensuring fair AI-driven decision-making.

We examined the Wess-Zumino model through the lens of bootstrap methods in four-dimensional space, incorporating the three-point vertices responsible for monodromy anomalies in the conformal bootstrap equation. These anomalies arise due to the non-trivial transformation of the model's fields under conformal changes. To circumvent these issues, we redefined the bootstrap equation in terms of correlators involving an additional compensator field, effectively rendering it free of problems, and then set this field to a specific value to obtain correlators of the model's original fields. Leveraging this approach, we derived a rigorous no-go theorem that prohibits the existence of conformal field theories with non-vanishing three-point interactions, a criterion that we applied to disprove the existence of Wess-Zumino models with exothermic potentials. Furthermore, we explored the parameters of the model's potentials, employing a lattice representation to perform numerical analyses, and executed the bootstrap bootstrap bootstrap to establish a lower limit on the scaling dimension of the potential's local maximum, demonstrating that it cannot surpass the model's R-charge scaling dimension.

We have discovered an infinite number of infinite families of elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ with points of a specific order, originating from $C_3$-extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$. Our findings suggest that these curves possess a specific property related to the levels being the product of distinct primes forming an arithmetic progression with a difference of six. Through non-exhaustive testing, we have also established an infinite number of exceptional cases with levels equal to a prime number or product of two distinct primes.

This study investigates how medium access methods influence channel estimation channel estimation quality and, consequently, error performance and error correction capabilities in next-generation error-resilient communication systems. To address this issue, we conduct theoretical and practical evaluations of stochastic medium access, such as slotted ALOHA and contention-based medium access, to understand the interference correlation and its statistical effects on channel estimation. Building on these insights, we develop a novel and efficient estimator to counteract interference, a novel mutual interference cancellation estimator and, such mutual interference cancellation, to enhance channel estimation performance. Our results show that the proposed estimator can statistically cancel interference and that it surpasses current channel estimation methods in terms of channel estimation quality and error correction capabilities.

Enhancing a node's features through graph convolutional networks (GCNs) has become the primary approach in various graph-related tasks that rely on labeling data. Nevertheless, obtaining labels for node data often incurs significant costs, rendering supervised GCN methods impractical in many cases. To overcome this obstacle, semi-supervised graph learning techniques have been developed, which combine labeled (supervised) data with numerous unlabeled (pseudo-labeled) node labels as additional training constraints. Yet, these approaches are hindered by two significant issues: (1) unreliable pseudo-labels that can undermine the performance of semi-supervised GCNs and (2, noisy data graphs that can impede the supervised learning process. To tackle these challenges, this study introduces a pioneering pseudo-labeling strategy called node-wise entropy minimization (NEM) to refine the accuracy of node labels and the node flow regularization (NFR) technique to purify noisy data graphs. By integrating NEM and NFR, we propose a new method called node-assisted graph cleaning (NAGC), which not only boosts the accuracy of pseudo-labels but also eliminates noise, thereby ultimately enhancing the performance of semi-supervised GCNs. Experiments on real-world graph datasets have validated the efficacy of NAGC in combating the problems associated with noisy data graphs and pseudo-labels.

We introduce PatchNet, a neural network architecture designed for video processing,
leveraging local template matching, and offer an efficient and compact solution
for video neural networks. Unlike global template matching, our approach of
leverage local templates within the forward pass of a neural network offers
significant alignment efficiency and performance boost. Our patch-based design
enables the use of low-rank additional parameters, resulting in a scalable and
efficient architecture for video processing. We explore the influence of our
alignment strategy on the forward pass of a neural network, developing a
two-stage training pipeline that achieves high-performant and lightweight models.
We also devise a technique to seamlessly integrate our patch-based additional
parameters into existing model architectures, facilitating the efficient
development of compact models for video datasets. We evaluate PatchNet on
datasets for video classification, achieving strong performance while models are
up to 14.6 times smaller and requiring 7.4 times fewer computations compared
to their non-aligned counterparts.

We modify the one-dimensional discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process by introducing $k-1$ additional site exclusion rules, resulting in a model where a single occupancy site is allowed for groups of up to $k$ consecutive particles. A stochastic update mechanism based on independent random walks is used to determine whether a particle moves or stays in place, similar to the method in the original exclusion process. A thorough mathematical analysis of the model's multi-point behavior is presented, including calculations of $n$-point correlation functions and density for both open and periodic boundary conditions. Notably, we obtain closed-form equations for these correlation functions, demonstrating that they can be expressed as products of terms related to the model's parameters, including initial conditions. These results are further validated by comparing our calculations with computer simulations, including an investigation into how changing model parameters affects the model's behavior.

A novel wireless power transfer method known as simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) has the potential to revolutionize the development of green wireless systems. This paper explores a SWIPT-enabled orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA) network where a base station allocates power to various services, including file transfer, video streaming, and live streaming. By considering energy-efficient resource allocation, this study maximizes the system's overall throughput while ensuring each service meets its minimum energy consumption requirements. To solve the associated optimization problem, we employ a step-by-step iterative approach involving linear programming and one-dimensional search. This approach guarantees a practical and optimal solution with guaranteed performance within a factor of $4/3$. Furthermore, to address the computational intensity of the proposed method, we introduce an alternative scheme that trades off energy efficiency for lower computational complexity. This new method, in turn, is optimized to maximize energy efficiency while minimizing the number of power variables. Numerical results demonstrate that SWIPT, with its ability to transmit both data and power over a single frequency subcarrier, significantly enhances system energy efficiency compared to traditional wireless power transfer. Additionally, the proposed OFDMA SWIPT system exhibits better performance than time-division multiple access (TDD) SWIPT in terms of energy efficiency.

We present a simple electrical circuit model of superconducting DR-mechanical oscillators that accurately reflects the impact of the radiative reaction force. Our findings indicate that the circuit's equivalent inductance can be interpreted as the mechanical oscillator's mass, the equivalent capacitance as its compliance, and the resistive component as the damping force. Furthermore, we demonstrate that energy dissipation in the mechanical system results from ohmic heating in the transducer, which is influenced by both the circuit and the mechanical motion. Our model also takes into account the recoil effect and shows that radiation pressure can be represented as a coupled RLC system, providing insight into the reciprocal forces acting on the circuit and the mechanical motion.

The definition and key properties of universal Airy polynomials are presented here. It's shown that the norm of universal Airy polynomials grows exponentially. Moreover, for any given degree n, there exists an infinite subset of the natural numbers with the characteristic that when k is from this subset and n is less than or equal to k, the leading coefficient of the kth orthogonal polynomial equals the leading coefficient of the nth universal Airy polynomial.

A common challenge in developing autonomous guided vehicles is the difficulty of navigating corners in warehouses, as most path-planning algorithms struggle with this task. To bypass this issue, researchers typically rely on wall-following techniques, although this method has its own complications - as vehicles often struggle to adapt to changes in wall directions, resulting in unstable movements known as "unruly shifts." This paper presents an in-depth analysis of unruly shifts, aiming to understand their underlying mechanics. It proposes a quantitative measure for assessing the severity of these shifts, called the Unruly Shift Index, and offers practical recommendations to mitigate their effects, including a heuristic approach for selecting the direction of traversal. Furthermore, the study demonstrates how Unruly Shifts can be predicted through data, using the index itself, and showcases the benefits of sharing this information across a fleet of AGVs to facilitate knowledge transfer and improve performance on wall-following tasks. The findings are validated through comparative field tests of a sample-based learning method and traditional unruly shift-based techniques on a real warehouse, involving multiple and varied turns, as well as shifts of varying degrees of difficulty.

This article explores the concepts of a notion of chirality within 2d fully algebraic quantum field theory, employing algebraic methods to do so.  It defines causal elements as either left- or right-going, and examines how these elements interact using a commutator.  It then establishes a connection between these elements' 'causal functions' through an examination of their transmission, and also connects this to the front factor formulation.  It's shown that the various approaches are equivalent.  It's also demonstrated that the 'causal functions' can be related to solutions of the massless Dirac equation, and that they form representations of the Dirac matrices, which correspond to the ones found in the Dirac equation.

Our research focuses on using image improvement techniques to assist in identifying smoke images during laparoscopic surgery. We identified that smoke is commonly used in minimally invasive surgery to temporarily obscure the camera lens, making recognition challenging. Our team hypothesized that applying image improvement techniques could facilitate easier recognition of smoke. We gathered 332 images from three different laparoscopic surgical systems and applied four widely accepted techniques, evaluating their effectiveness with subjective and objective metrics. Our findings revealed that image improvement can enhance visibility, but it also alters the appearance of smoke, potentially affecting its recognition.

We investigate the development of controlled two-qubit interactions utilizing the Molmer-Sorensen gate, focusing on the role of motional mode dissipation. To mitigate losses affecting different motional modes to unequal extents, our design of controlled forces involves equal coupling to all modes, thus minimizing the impact of losses and preserving the fidelity. We further investigate how non-uniform loss affects performance and investigate strategies to compensate for non-uniformities in the master equation, specifically in the context of drift effects, within a single ion quantum computer setting.

We present a novel method involving the substitution of lanthanum ions with ions of varying polarizing capacities in the structure of lanthanum zirconate. This innovative approach enables the examination of the impact of electric dipoles on a material's structural properties. By utilizing neutron and x-ray diffraction, we've identified the presence of specific atomic position distortions associated with polar lanthanum ions, which are characteristic of ferroelectric and pyroelectric materials. Furthermore, our research employs a novel framework rooted in group-subgroup relationships to systematically investigate material characteristics, particularly the characteristics associated with atomic displacements. This research demonstrates the utility of our methodology in determining properties of materials in various states, and particularly in the vicinity of a material's phase transition point.

Multivariate data often exhibit correlations that change across different conditions, which can be captured by a conditional Gaussian process (CGP). The use of CGPs allows researchers to model complex patterns of dependence in data sets, particularly when those patterns are associated with a continuous variable such as time or frequency. Theoretical advancements in areas like Function-on-Scalar regression (FoS) and Graphical FS (FoS with regression) have led to the development of graphical Gaussian processes (GGPs), which enable researchers to analyze the correlation structures within datasets more effectively. This study builds upon existing work by theoretically connecting GGP components to their FoS and Graphical FS counterparts, which in turn allows researchers to gain a deeper understanding of the connection between the spatio-temporal Gaussian process (STGP) approach used in GGP (Rasmussen and Williams, 2006) and the more general Function-on-Vector regression (FovV) model. The study's findings have been implemented in a new extension of the {ggp} R package, which allows researchers to efficiently estimate Graphical FS models using the {mgcv} R package (Wood, 2013). This streamlined approach to GGP estimation holds the potential to be applied to a broader range of applications, including Graphical FS models with interactions, which has so far been theoretically challenging due to the need to perform complex and computationally intensive operations on large datasets.

Predictability in a quantum computing system is essential due to the inherently unpredictable nature of some operations. This study defines predictable algorithms for compiling circuits with built-in architecture that focuses on repeating patterns, utilizing a novel method called match-growth.

To address the problem of adding necessary gates within repeating patterns to meet a specific unitary update, we introduce a solution called the match-growth algorithm. This solution is both optimal and can be applied efficiently with a time complexity of $O(n \log n)$. Furthermore, we integrate the match-growth algorithm with existing strategies to create a new, predictable circuit compiler for NISQ devices with dedicated build-in architectures, specifically designed for Gaussian states preparation. This new compiler, PQA, achieves optimal performance on a test dataset of Gaussian states, outdoing other approaches in efficiency by a significant margin, while also proving its effectiveness on a non-repeating patterns test case.

The primary focus of this research is an enhanced, average-case version of the convex Riemann hypothesis, which is a result derived from a 1999 paper by Keating and Soundararajan. This average-case formulation yields a more robust and precise outcome. Specifically, this paper examines the distribution of normalized keystone functions, which is a metric employed in the 2021 derivation. The study aims to elucidate how the convexity assumption influences the behavior of the convective function, and in the absence of this assumption, it investigates the behavior of the convective function. The investigation into average-case and strong versions of the convex Riemann hypothesis provides insight into the nature of the complex plane's critical values. Additionally, this research includes numerical data that validates the new, average-case formula.

Our study delves into the impact of interlayer distance and electron-hole interaction strength on the lower energy states of a double-layered excitonic insulator. Through numerical calculations, we determine the lower root of the mean field equations, which serve as the ground state of many-body interactions, to obtain the lower band structure. Furthermore, we use a self-consistent approach to compute the higher energy states, which are then compared with the lower energy states to identify the excitation gap. Our analysis shows that increasing the coupling strength or decreasing the interlayer distance results in the closure of the excitation gap. To model this gap closure, we employ a simple polymer approximation. Our findings also indicate that the excitation gap's rate of decrease is heavily influenced by the coupling of electrons and holes, with this effect being amplified as this coupling increases.

This work presents an innovative, self-calibrating and adaptive passive localization and tracking (PLT) approach designed specifically for environments with obstacles that cause significant Doppler shifts. The approach leverages a two-tier network structure, with a controller overseeing a cluster of user-equipment (UE) and a set of radio-frequency (RF) communication transfer agents (CTAs). Each CTA is responsible for assisting one specific UE, and their intelligent reflection capabilities help mitigate the impact of obstacles by reflecting a signal from the gateway. The PLT algorithm utilizes a communication transfer-based channel estimation method to accurately capture a Ute's trajectory over time. The CTA's reflective beams help maintain continuous communication with the gateway, and the controller's adaptive selection of CTA's ensures optimal performance. The approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through comparative results with a traditional method.

We describe a novel technique for discerning the polarization states of gauge bosons produced in proton-proton collisions. Our approach employs the full orientation of the bosons' decay products and their decay patterns, captured by novel kinematic variables. We present initial results from $W^{\pm}Z$ production at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy, assuming the standard model. Our findings are based on $ATLAS$ data collected with a 25 fb$^{-1}$ integrated luminosity, processed to identify the complete polarization states of the bosons using the $W$'s transverse polarization and the $Z$'s longitudinal polarization. We observe that the joint-polarization rates align with theoretical predictions within one standard deviation, with notable multiple interference effects between the $W$ and $Z$ bosons observed at 2.2 standard deviations.

We suggest an alternative framework for describing gravity, based on the Cotton-York vector in three dimensions, which becomes the Cotton tensor when formulated as a 2-form in four dimensions, representing the dual of the Cotton-York vector. This approach enables a direct dual relationship between the Weyl tensor and the Cotton tensor, allowing us to show that the latter disregards changes in scale. Furthermore, the condition that the Weyl tensor equates to zero corresponds directly to (1) the absence of scale alterations, (2 a unique relationship between the Riemann tensor, (2b) a zero scale change in the Riemann tensor, (3) the space being conformally equivalent to a space with zero scale in its Riemann tensor. This equivalence also results in the space being conformally equivalent to the product of hyperbolic and Euclidean spaces.

Banaschewski and Wickel provided a dual representation theorem for the collection of topological spaces and continuous functions in their 1980 paper. Boulders and Delfs reworked this theorem specifically for ortholattices in 2009, and we have further refined this lattice version to work for orthomodular lattices, yielding a more generalized version of Boulders and Delfs' original theorem. As a consequence, we obtain distinct dual representations of orthomodular lattices, thereby extending previously established results by Janssen and Dickson, as well as Boulders and Delfs.

We present Coq-psv, a proof diagram visualisation tool built on top of coq-psv. Coq-psv takes proof diagrams as input, which we use to illustrate the structure of coq proof terms with multiple levels of abstraction. Coq-psv can also accept coq proof terms directly as input, automatically parsing them into proof diagrams in the process. Coq-psv serves as a suitable substitute for coq-proof-viewer, while Coq-psv provides an additional layer of proof term abstraction over coq-proof-viewer. Coq-psv is implemented in JavaScript.

In a specific range of parameters for a particular type of mathematical function, we determine the precise upper limit for the average of its fourth power in the spectral domain. This upper limit matches, within a constant factor, the best known limit for the average of the function's spectral coefficients raised to the fourth power. We achieve this result by applying a particular identity, known as the Rademacher mean value formula, to the spectral expansion of a set of functions known as Hecke cusp forms, and then apply the Poincaré-Siegel formula to obtain the result.

Interior Point Methods (IPMs), a subset of Elliptic Optimization Methods, are employed to address Charnes-Cooper and quadratic reformulations of Convex Quadratic Programming problems. As part of the IPM process, precision-seeking algorithms are utilized to determine the optimal solution; specifically, Krylov solvers are frequently applied due to their computational efficiency. However, the efficiency of these algorithms is hindered by their iterative nature and associated overhead, necessitating a highly accurate termination criterion. Currently, criteria such as residual, divergence, and failure are utilized to determine when to halt iteration, but they may not be suitable for all scenarios. This research proposes a novel termination criterion that incorporates the affine and Newton search directions to assess the feasibility of convergence, thereby offering a more accurate assessment of the optimal solution. This proposed criterion is tested against traditional termination criteria through numerical simulations and demonstrates its potential to improve the IPM performance, particularly for problems reformulated using the Charnes-Cooper method and others that involve conic quadratic constraints. The effectiveness of the new criterion is evaluated based its ability to decrease the number of necessary iterations, making it a promising tool for enhancing IPM efficiency.

We have computed the first-order correction to the singlet quark-to-glueon transition matrix element ($A_{gq}$) in the variable flavor number scheme (VFS) of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at order $\alpha_s^3$ for five-flavor and five-favor schemes. The leading-order and next-to-leading-order contributions to $A_{gq}$ in the five-flavor scheme are reviewed, along with new results for the next-to-next-to-leading order (NLLS) and two-flavor scheme's next-to-next-to-leading order (NXTL) and five-flavor scheme's NLLS. The calculations for $A_{gq}$ in the two-flavor and five-flavor schemes involve solving inhomogeneous differential equations for the operator matrix elements. These are integrated with the two-loop splitting functions in the respective schemes and incorporate the one-loop contribution from the four-flavor scheme.
