Data mining and knowledge discovery have led to a significant interest in association rules, a concept that has multiple definitions, each with its own advantages and limitations. This paper expands upon the work of Grossi et al., offering a revised framework for association rules to address gaps in their original theory. The proposed framework is based on a logical deduction structure, providing formal proofs for issues that were previously only addressed through heuristics, such as finding the smallest set of association rules that can derive a given set of rules. This study focuses on the concept of axiomatic association rules, defining them as the minimal set of rules that can deduce a given target rule, with further classification into symmetrical and restrictive subsets. Experimental results indicate that finding a minimal base of rules is an NP-hard problem, and various algorithms, such as a heuristic algorithm and parameterized algorithms, have been explored to address this challenge.

The number of people going through the criminal justice system is rising, resulting in a significant number needing mental health support. Despite this, access to such services is limited, largely due to declining funding for mental health care. Criminal justice offenders frequently experience low levels of such support, contributing to higher rates of recidivism, relapse, and a greater risk of future crimes. To address a critical gap in the literature, this study investigates the effects of mandated mental health care on recurrence, prescription drug use, and the commission of future crimes. We analyze a large dataset from Texas, and find that mandated therapy has a notable positive impact, reducing recurrence and a range of adverse outcomes, with little to no effect on prescription drug use or new crimes. We speculate that mandated mental health care contributes to improved outcomes, but require further research to fully understand the underlying mechanisms at play.

The authors introduce a new class of Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters and derive their key properties, including relationships with other special numbers and coefficients, as well as an associated infinite series. They also obtain the generating functions for these parameters and related sums.

This paper explores the concept of autonomous drone-based spectrum exploration to create radio maps, which involve flying drones to measure and analyze the wireless environment at close range. Our research showcases the feasibility of this approach with real-world experiments using multi-rotor drones equipped with cognitive radio technology to assess the coverage and performance of wireless networks. These experiments utilized a grid-based flight path and a collaborative strategy where one drone flies, another measures, and a third computes the radio map, as demonstrated in a test of this protocol.

Real-time monitoring and predictive maintenance in industrial settings require the capability to detect irregular behavior. Although. in our research, we developed a novel, model-free, real-time anomaly detection framework for SCADA systems in power plants. This system leverages hidden Markov models (HMMs) to assess gauge readings and pinpoint anomalies. By utilizing an online algorithm, our model automatically trains on normal system behavior and remains dynamic, adapting to changes without manual intervention. This approach enables the evaluation of individual and collective system malfunctions, as well as the identification of faults during system transitions. Evaluation with actual plant data demonstrates the system's effectiveness in detecting anomalies, with an identification accuracy of 85% - 95%.

This study explores the effectiveness of combining audio-visual-thermal sensors for unique person verification, using a publicly accessible dataset from the Audio-Visual-Thermal Challenge 2019. Visually capturing facial features during speaking adds to image reliability while thermal sensing for the same facial aspects increases performance at all times while speaking. Our experimentation demonstrates that the combined modality works best, surpassing the other individual and combined systems from the challenge in various conditions.

We propose a method to minimize the effort in increasing the size of training data by applying a two-practice approach in sequence. Firstly, we convert spoken language into a more rich and expressive form by creating a sentence graph, which allows us to preserve the temporal sequence of audio while adding non-word level nodes. Secondly, we apply the same method of virtual duplication to these sentence graphs, a technique previously applied to sequences of words. We applied this method to automatic speech recognition and machine translation tasks using virtual duplication with variations of random insertion and substitution. Experimental results indicate that the size of the training data can be reduced by up to 10 times without affecting the performance of the models.

Consider a finite population of size N denoted as {y_1,...,y_N}, where some elements y_i are classified as successes and others as failures. Some elements are accessible at a cost of c_i, denoted as {c_i: i in I_N}, where I_N is a subset of {1,...,N}. The objective is to identify the proportion of successes among the N elements in the population at a cost of c, denoted as p(c). In this research, a generalized form of the average of parameters for a finite population is presented and the parameter space and estimator for p(c) are determined. The variance of these estimators is also investigated and some applications are demonstrated.

Building on the concept of differential privacy, we introduce a new framework called one-sided differential privacy (SDP), which is suitable for scenarios where a particular data party acts in good faith. Our investigation into SDP reveals that the strict definition leads to trivial outcomes, thus we adopt a more lenient version. Furthermore, we show that the relaxed definition permits a trade-off between the accuracy of aggregate data and the protection of individual confidential information. Unlike differential privacy, the relaxed SDP offers only partial confidentiality for certain characteristics of a data subject, as it depends on their attributes. To address this limitation, we introduce a new metric for quantifying confidence on a probabilistic scale, called one-sided differential guarantee (SDG). The SDG can be computed efficiently using vector representations of datasets, and we also explore its connection to information theory.

We have obtained high-resolution gas and dust maps of the AS 209 gas giant's protoplanetary disk. The high-density regions in the dust map correspond to multiple ring structures, with the presence of a cavity at the center, which is filled with gas but devoid of dust, similar to other systems with gas trapping mechanisms. Although the radial structures of gas and dust align at the outer edges, they diverge near the cavity, where gas density remains constant while dust density increases. This pattern could be explained by gas pressure support preventing dust from settling into the cavity, or by trapping the gas and processing it through photochemistry, which would prevent the dust from settling as well.

To analyze time series data accurately, having access to reliable, user-friendly, and versatile software tools is essential. An analysis suite is available at no cost on our website (https://phys.ksu.edu/~tsf/toolkit/), offering a selection of a priori and adaptive examination methods, including both efficient and more computationally demanding, as well as flexible, customized analysis methods. The toolkit features a time series analysis module, enabling analysis of a wide range of phenomena, from radiation decay and statistical accumulations to the movement of individual particles and the behavior of chains, all of which are subject to time constraints. The results of these analyses can be graphically displayed, and parameters, such as diffusion coefficients and relaxation times, can be determined. The toolkit's output graphs can be compared to theoretical predictions, and any deviations from expected results can be quantified, and possible reasons for these discrepancies can be identified. The analysis suite supports a variety of examination methods, and all its tools, as well as its results, are compatible with the latest version of Microsoft Office.

This paper considers a type of mean field games with controlled dynamics and state restrictions, where the existence of "mild solutions" is proven for a class of non-regular problems. The analysis involves minimizing an integral cost function over time with terminal state constraints. Specifically, we consider state constraints that satisfy a robust monotone path independence condition, and our results show the existence of equilibria in mixed strategies for a broad class of compact state constraints. Our analysis builds on the concept of Hamiltonian trajectories and uses methods such as verification of coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-isometric equations and Fokker-Planck equations.

Recent high-precision data from the Gaia data release 2 reveals an unusual pattern in the movement of stars within the galaxy, centered in the plane, characterized by an elliptical shape. This dynamic pattern is seen across a wide range of distances from the center, exhibits specific variations in speed, and is associated with stars that have specific movement attributes. This striking phenomenon is observed among stars that make up approximately 10% of the central stars in the Gaia data set, implying that it could be more widespread within the galaxy's central area. Although multiple theoretical models attempt to explain this phenomenon, no single model has yet to provide a comprehensive explanation. This review aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the features of this stellar pattern, discuss the features of various models that try to explain it, and offer recommendations for future research to better understand its underlying mechanics.

Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the rise of visual discovery detection, leading to the creation of multiple trained models capable of identifying visual patterns in images. However, current methods are largely limited to visual tasks that can be learned from general image datasets, such as VGG-SN or ImageNet, and often fail to effectively identify discrepancies within specific sub-categories. Furthermore, these models are unable to effectively learn differences within highly similar items within the same category, such as clothing. To address these challenges, this research presents Visual Discrepancy Detection with Transformers, which leverages pre-trained fashion contrastive models to effectively learn and identify visual discrepancies within item-specific datasets. By incorporating the FauxMIMU, a pre-trained fashion contrastive model, Visual Discrepancy Detection with Transformers overcomes the limitations of multiple discrepancy patterns, such as those found in QuadTree80, and avoids the issue of under-training, such as that observed in VGG-SN and ResNet50. By leveraging the domain expertise of FauxMIMU, Visual Discrepancy Detection with Transformers achieves superior performance in multiple discrepancy detection tasks, such as those found in QuadTree80 and ImageNet.

Recent advancements in quantum technology have sparked growing interest in the systematic study of quantum resource theories. The distinction between classical and quantum behaviors is the fundamental premise of the most fundamental resource theory. However, the limitations of the binary framework have led researchers to explore more sophisticated settings, such as the photon number resolving scenario. Recent research has focused on the potential of photon numbers as a measure of quantumness and the structure of the associated resource theory. We aim to provide a comprehensive overview of these new findings. The paper will discuss the theoretical framework of the most minimal resource theory, its experimental implications, and potential applications. Additionally, we will examine other more complex resource theories that incorporate photon indistinguishability.

In modern federated learning, utilizing various devices with distinct characteristics to train global models, managing the non-stationary nature of distributed data becomes a significant concern. The asynchronous accumulation (AA) method, which is not bound by device synchronization, has shown potential in mitigating this issue. However, prior to this, a key limitation of this approach, namely the stationary assumption of data, was identified. This paper takes steps to address this concern by analyzing the impact of asynchronous training and device heterogeneity on global model performance. The research focuses on unconstrained gradient updates in the Federated Learning (FL) setting and allows for the possibility of globally unique optimal solutions. The study assumes that the FL network operates in an asynchronous, device-heterogeneous environment, with the number of updates and participating devices varying each round. The results indicate that the buffered AA FL with uniquely optimal solutions and i.i.d. data achieves the same convergence rate as synchronous methods, with the most significant influence of the buffer size and device Heter- $\mathcal{D}$-expectation on the convergence rate. The theoretical findings also extend to non-i.i.d. data and unconstrained gradient updates in Federated Learning, with the influence of data variance and the FL network structure on the convergence rate being highlighted. The research provides constructive buffer size suggestions with numerical verification and further validates the method's efficacy on real-world datasets such as CIFAR-10 and Shaker.

This study investigates a joint operational calculus within the framework of a specific distribution space, a subset of the Schwartz space, comprising polynomial tempered distributions and their linear combinations with monomials of increasing degree, specifically related to the derivative of the Dirac delta at zero. We demonstrate that the space T'p is equivalent to the Fourier image of the space C^{\infty}, of C^{\infty}-functions, of an entire infinite dimensional C^{\infty}-function algebra. A key point of this research lies in examining a joint operational calculus, using a time derivative in the context of a dual space of a finite-dimensional C^{\infty}_c functions, with respect to an n-dimensional Euclidean space, where n is a positive integer, and applying it to the distribution space T'p. A crucial component of this study lies in defining the joint Fourier transform of a vector of tempered distributions.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has kept some forms of primordial black holes (PBHs) as viable options for at least a portion of the universe's matter due to the lack of inconsistencies discovered with observations of the dark sector. However, new findings on low-frequency gravitational waves from LIGO and Virgo have further restricted PBH models as a matter explanation. We demonstrate that the Shadow Dark Matter model, a potential extension of the Standard Model of particle physics, naturally incorporates a substantial portion of PBHs and provides an alternative to fine-tuning. The Shadow Dark Matter model's strong coupling to PBHs avoids certain contradictions with LIGO and Virgo data, making it a promising approach in explaining dark matter and related phenomena, including inflation, without violating both theoretical and observational constraints.

Scientific research indicates that biological membranes, such as cell coats, exhibit properties similar to solids due to their organized molecular structure. When these membranes become stretched beyond their optimal area, they transition into larger, crystalline-like domains. Our team has discovered and studied new methods for creating stress in model cell structures, known as tethers and multi-domain vesicles, to understand how they fracture. Our experiments reveal that the membrane's response to stress is consistent across different shapes and does not decrease over time, as anticipated by a theory of flexible membrane adaptation. Instead, the experiment's results support a theory of stable membrane structure.

The main challenge in maximizing the potential of gallium nitride is its limited strain, which hinders the enhancement of its performance. In this study, researchers discovered a method to expand the achievable strain to over 6% by integrating a GaN layer with a binary nitride material in a quantum well or a quaternary nitride. By either using ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ as a lattice-matched barrier or a lattice-matched nitride material, a 300% increase in the mobility of electrons or holes was observed at a 2% sheet carrier density in comparison to conventional AlN barriers or suspended GaN channels, with superior thermal conductivity in ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ to AlN or suspended GaN channels providing an added advantage. Simulation results suggest that the exceptional mobility observed experimentally is a result of the anisotropic strain in GaN, leading to band structure modifications and a 40% reduction in the ionized impurity scattering rate resulting from growth-related defects. These findings suggest that the enhanced mobility and strain tolerance offered by ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ can yield performance improvements in power devices and high-electron-mobility transistors.

Our research focuses on developing an efficient navigation strategy for marine robots using intrinsic variation in the environment to minimize path lengths. A novel method is introduced that leverages intrinsic regulation of the robot's velocity, derived from the intrinsic axis of motion, to optimize navigation in areas with inherent environmental fluctuation. To facilitate this, we employ the Gaussian process model to model the fluctuation patterns, and then select the intrinsic axis based on the most reliable data points. To address computational limitations, we develop a simplified structure for the covariance function using the kernel's spectral decomposition, and further optimize the process using variational approximation. We verify the efficacy of our approach through experimental results obtained from a robot navigating an underwater warehouse.

We establish new formulas for the Darboux and Calapso transformations of isothermal surfaces in a four-dimensional Euclidean space, assuming the Gauss map is meromorphic. This leads to identifying the class of isothermal surfaces with a meromorphic Gauss map as the Lawson surfaces when the Darboux transformation is set to the identity. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the Lawson surfaces generated by a given isothermal surface and the related null curve it forms.

This paper proposes a new method for estimating a conditional expectation function with no assumptions about its characteristics. The method involves selecting a set of functions to approximate the expected value of a function of vectors. The proposed estimator is both asymptotically efficient and versatile, making it particularly useful in settings such as analyzing choice functions under cardinal and ordinal utility assumptions. The results are also relevant for other conditions, like the Imbens-Topel identification of black box models. The framework is further illustrated by examples that explore bias and variance in kernel-based estimators and show how estimation errors can be reduced through function selection.

Let $r$ be a nonnegative integer and consider the set partitioning integer linear combinations of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ into $j$ groups with each containing no more than $r$ integers. We denote the coefficients for these combinations as $\lambda$-versions of the $r$-Stirling numbers of the second type and will explore their properties. Our goal is to derive identities related to these numbers by examining their relationships with the standard Stirling numbers of the second type. Additionally, we will define the $\lambda$-bosonic numbers of the second type in terms of a specific polynomial and present relevant identities that arise from its key properties.

Predicting missing relationships in evolving knowledge graphs, known as the link forecasting challenge, has numerous real-world applications. Traditional approaches often rely on sophisticated models that can be difficult to execute temporally. In contrast, this paper explores the effectiveness of static predictive frameworks in addressing this challenge. Temporal networks are modeled as a sequence of snapshots, analyzed statistically, and evaluated for their ability to forecast relationships over time. We adapted the logistic regression and random forest classifiers for use with temporal networks, comparing their performance against established baselines and existing solutions. Notably, our results show that the logistic regression achieved the best balance of efficiency and effectiveness, surpassing the baseline methods and matching the performance of more complex models in multiple datasets.

We examine the concept of robust equivalence for countable graph systems and associated C*-algebras, defining it as a relationship between finite graphs and C*-algebras respectively. It is proven that robust equivalence for graphs implies shift equivalence for the associated C*-algebras, a result that also indicates robust equivalence is preserved under graph C*-algebra Morita equivalence, a contribution that precedes the findings in [1]. Moreover, we demonstrate that two countable graph systems are robustly equivalent if and only if their associated C*-algebras are strongly shift equivalent via P-equivalence C*-algebras, a concept also explored in [1].

In the presence of an intense magnetic field, the production and dispersion of quarks within a QCD medium are altered, and the parameters of the medium can be examined through observations of quark-jets at collider experiments. Field strength in the early universe or neutron stars may significantly impact quark behavior. Employing the gauge invariant self-energy method and a magnetic field finite quark-propagator approach, and incorporating color dipole formalism, researchers calculated the complex trajectory of a heavy quark, and this trajectory is used to construct propagator for calculating the produced hadron's correlator. Utilizing the generated propagator, the distribution of heavy hadrons is determined, and both energy and transverse momentum heavy hadron spectra are computed and Anisotropy in the fragmentation process is evaluated as influenced by the magnetic field and thermal conditions.

Recent advancements in natural language processing, particularly with pre-trained language models like BERT, have significantly improved task performance. However, research indicates that integrating knowledge graphs can further enhance models' problem-solving capabilities, especially in question-answering tasks. Although several studies have explored this integration, they have relied on basic knowledge graph relations without exploring more advanced reasoning capabilities. In contrast, this study examines the benefits of using a sophisticated knowledge graph reasoning system, ReCoR, in language model pre-training and fine-tuning for question-answering tasks. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating ReCoR substantially improves language models, yielding the best results on two datasets, yielding scores of 71.7 and 75 on the TREC question-answering dataset, with a 10-point improvement over the current best score.

Graph expander networks from vertex-to-vertex connected graphs have achieved significant success in various areas such as computer science, combinatorics, and physics. They are particularly valuable in these domains. However, their application is limited in higher dimensions due to certain inherent constraints. We have discovered a novel class of high-dimensional expander graphs derived from connected graphs, which surpasses traditional methods in terms of expandability and versatility. Our research shows that these new expanders have a remarkable property of maintaining high expandability in their $k$-skeletons when $k$ is sufficiently large, specifically up to $\Omega(\log d)$.

Recent advancements in natural language processing have brought about a surge in interest towards prompts, enabling models to efficiently execute an array of tasks, including classification tasks, without requiring additional training. Our research delves into the effectiveness of utilizing prompts in classification settings, aiming to answer the question of whether prompts can effectively substitute traditional classification approaches. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of prompts' potential to replace traditional classification methods, encompassing scenarios where prompts either incorporate labeled data or function without it. We also investigate the effects of incorporating different data types on prompt performance, including varied classification formats. Ultimately, our findings indicate that prompts, in conjunction with pre-trained language models, can match the accuracy of trained classifiers, 3.5% better perform than choice models with pre-trained parameters, and 4.6% better perform choice models with trained parameters.

Building on previous work by Deligne and Beilinson, we define the L-invariants associated with Artin motivations with finite-order actions, as well as lower, mixed l-adic realizations. Our results can be seen as extensions to Artin motivations of findings by Blasius regarding the l-adic realizations of extreme weights modular forms. Moreover, by combining with prior work by Chang and Srinivasan on the motivic Bloch-Ellenberg-Floyd elements, we obtain explicit expressions for the periods of key Artin motivations.

In atomic quantum information processing, detecting diffracted microwave fields from Rydberg atoms is a crucial step. This process forms the basis for microwaves detection, entanglement generation, and gate operations. However, conventional methods suffer from low detection efficiencies due to limitations imposed by system settings and system scale. We've developed an innovative approach leveraging machine learning techniques to enhance these methods. By模拟模拟 the scattering process and training a classifier to recognize patterns in simulated data, we've developed an efficient classifier capable of accurately identifying the Rabi oscillations within raw simulation data, thus setting a new standard for detection efficiency at. Furthermore, we've shown that our method outperforms traditional techniques, even when accounting for real-world system imperfections, by surpassing an efficiency of.

UGC8839, an exceptional spiral galaxy, boasts a remarkable constant thickness of 5.3% across its entire disc. This thickness remains一致 from its largest radius of 36.5 kpc all the way down to its central region, where it's approximately 10 times thinner than at its edges. UC8839's light distribution features a very faint, compact bulge, prominently bright inner arms, and a prominent flare in its disc. Notably, UC8839's velocity field exhibits a significant rotation, with a Halpha-based measurement of 164 km/s. Using a specialized model, we've determined that UC8839's mass-to-light ratio is 0.44 M_sun/L_sun at its edges and 0.34 M_sun/L_sun in its central region. UC8839's constant thickness suggests a dynamic equilibrium between gravitational forces, rather than indicating steady-state conditions.

This dissertation investigates various aspects of quaseregular mappings R^n->R^n and their associated non-linear Cantor sets. The underlying measure, raised to the power of n, is utilized. We employ a novel method to demonstrate that the Hausdorff measure of regular mapping invariant sets is either zero or infinity. Additionally, we examine the conditions under which the Hausdorff measure of these invariant sets attains infinity. Furthermore, we investigate the properties of quasiregular mappings R^n-1->R^n-1, specifically their partial inverses. Using this analysis, we establish that the partial inverse of a quasiregular mapping constitutes a Carleson-quasiconformal function. Finally, leveraging these results, we construct a set with partial projection P^n-1 projections possessing distinct Hausdorff dimensions.

The discovery of Mars' atmospheric gravity waves dates back 15 years to measurements made by the Mars Global Surveyor. These waves cause the Tharsis region's ionized and neutral layers to respond to the planet's climatic fluctuations. The recent additions of data from the Mars Odyssey, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution Mission have greatly enhanced our knowledge of the gravity waves affecting Tharsis. The MGS, MRO, and MAVEN instruments have contributed in assessing the variations in electron density and total density deficiency due to total ionization disturbances in the Tharsis region. Similarly, the Mars Odyssey total neutron deficiency measurements have facilitated in locating the regions where the gravity waves impact Tharsis. The waves cause the Tharsis region's ionized and neutral layers to respond to the planet's climatic fluctuations using ionization deficiency, electron density deficiency, and total neutron deficiency as indicators. This study presents the latest research on gravity waves in the Tharsis region until 2018. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of multiple space missions in providing complementary data on the same phenomenon in the same region of the planet. The gravity waves cause the Tharsis region's ionized and neutral layers to respond to the planet's climatic fluctuations using deficiency as an indicator.

The LHC has demonstrated its capability for nucleus-nucleus collisions at a $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}} = 5.02$ TeV and for proton-nucleus collisions at 13 TeV. We explore the advantages of measuring forward charmonium production within Pb-Pb interactions. Recent research by the ALICE collaboration is presented, specifically concerning J/ψ production in Pb-Pb interactions at 25, 50, and 80 TeV, as well as in Pb-Pb ultra-peripheral interactions at 5, 10, and 20 TeV. We examine how this production method compares to other forward J/ψ measurement techniques, such as those involving photoproduction, and we present predictions for very high energy interactions at the future CLIC and FCC-ee/hh colliders, focusing on the influence of Pb-Pb geometry and forward charmonium production contributions.

In recent years, there has been significant interest in sound design techniques that utilize visual inputs to create audio through visual synthesis. However, visually inspired sound design techniques are largely restricted due to their automatic processes, which do not offer designers the flexibility to creatively manipulate sounds and customize their methods. To address this limitation, we introduce an interactive system that enables customized visually directed sound synthesis. Building upon the foundational DISS sound synthesis model, our system allows designers to establish a personalized connection between visual inputs and audio output, thereby making the process more flexible and adaptable. To showcase the potential of this system, we conducted a study involving designers who used it for their practical workflows, as well as a study with participants who employed it for their sound design projects, revealing its effectiveness and benefits.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are highly effective in addressing problems involving sequences, such as natural language processing, but they often require extensive data and struggle to effectively capture temporal patterns. To improve the representation of temporal patterns, researchers have proposed pre-training Recurrent Neural Network models using large amounts of unlabelled sequence data. In this research, we investigate the use of Recurrent Neural Networks for capturing temporal patterns in data that evolves over time. We acquire this knowledge by analyzing the behavior of recurrent neural networks when processing large volumes of unlabelled data. We assess the benefits of pre-training these models on multiple datasets, including machine translation, clickstream data, and disease diagnosis, and find that our approach consistently enhances the performance of downstream tasks that rely on temporal patterns.

To maintain public health and economic stability, the key factor is to implement precise and timely pandemic interventions, as supported by our analysis across multiple models. Furthermore, our assessment of model accuracy and validity reveals the extent to which different pandemic models can accurately predict outcomes and inform effective policy decisions.

The primary objective of this research is to introduce a Shapley value-based approach,
End-to-End significance over MACHLe (EML), to determine the importance of data items
through their effects on machine learning pipeline outcomes. Unlike existing Shapley value-based
methods that analyze their own particular contexts, EML can be applied to any machine learning pipeline
and accommodates various types of model components. Our approach also offers a novel framework
for any pipeline by treating machine learning pipelines as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and using
data troubleshooting and significance to examine individual data items' influences on pipeline performance.
We tested EML on various data items with issues across three datasets, showcasing its effectiveness
and versatility across different pipeline types.

This paper begins with two introductory sections on how to approach and organize complex topics. Drawing from experiences in training graduate students, it emphasizes the importance of hands-on learning through examples and encourages students to engage with others in the research community. The paper then explores how statistics, specifically intersection theory, has influenced modern algebraic geometry, particularly in enumerative geometry. A notable application of this field is mentioned, which involves counting geometric objects, and this has led to the development of powerful tools like Gromov-Witten invariants, providing solutions to long-standing problems in mathematics.

Research on materials exhibiting anomalous Hall effect (AHE) has garnered significant attention recently, particularly in systems with noncollinear magnetic arrangements. Although such systems often display antiferromagnetic behavior, which typically lacks large Hall resistivity, researchers have found the combination of noncollinear magnetism with other factors, like lattice distortions and magnetic interactions, can lead to phenomena involving both AHE and spin polarization. Our investigation centered on a novel Mott band magnet, Mn$_3$Sn, which possesses a triangular noncollinear arrangement, and we subjected it to high pressures up to 10 kbar. While a 0.6 percent compression resulted in a 300-fold increase in AME compared to ambient conditions, we discovered that this compression led to a transition where Mn$_3$Sn became more like a band magnet. This was accompanied by reduced band overlap and diminished interactions, ultimately causing the sample to transition into a ferromagnetic state at around 200 K under 10 kbar of pressure.

Recent Deep Neural Network (DNN) architectures have demonstrated exceptional performance in the task of relation extraction (RE). This chapter aims to provide a comprehensive overview of RE tasks, covering both explicit and implicit approaches. The analysis encompasses the advantages and limitations of various RE methods as well as potential directions for future research.

This paper examines a combined Steklov-Robin boundary value problem for the Laplacian operator, which yields a unique set of real eigenvalues and corresponding real eigenfunctions that form a complete orthonormal basis in the $L^2$ space. We study how the problem's boundary conditions and eigenvalue/eigenfunction properties are interconnected, and we analyze the problem using a specific function class and derive related inequalities, ultimately revealing the problem reduces to a particular weighted eigenvalue problem.

Hypergraph reconstruction focuses on deriving unobserved hyperedges from known ones in a hypergraph. Traditional approaches primarily generate random negative hyperedges to calculate distance metrics like the Ising model. Nonetheless, this method fails to accurately reflect real-world negative samples. We propose a two-phase hypergraph reconstruction technique. In the first phase, we generate improved potential negative edges by iteratively swapping switches between given hyperedges. We then utilize these edges to reconstruct missing links via the Ising model. Our experimental evaluations demonstrate that this algorithm outperforms existing methods in reconstructing unobserved hyperedges.

This study presents a dataset, CXR_CT, for evaluating chest X-ray readers. The CXR_CT dataset features 14,631 paired images: each chest X-ray image alongside its corresponding computed tomography projection. To supplement the CXR_CT dataset, a novel annotation system called CXR_XA was developed. The CXR_XA annotation system incorporates comprehensive understanding aids, comprising location, lesion type, and pathology description. A novel approach for producing CXR_XA annotations from gold standard reports and existing Findings + Labels + Assessment readings utilizes a combination of large language models and annotators. The involvement of human experts in CXR_XA generation has led to improved report understanding. The integration of a Swin Transformer model enabled the evaluation of CXR_XA and found abnormalities in 47% of additional cases. Furthermore, the analysis of CXR_XA has led to improved description accuracy, with the help of the understanding annotations.

We establish a relationship between Euler characteristics of tight contact structures on certain negative definite four-manifolds and the Thurston norm of their boundary's core. These four-manifolds are constructed by Dold using the concept of the Dixmier index map, which we also introduce and demonstrate to be -deterministic for the fundamental group of three-manifolds with a non-positive Euler characteristic. Our findings imply that the Thurston norm of the core is deterministic and, consequently, that tight contact structures corresponding to negative definite manifolds with non-positive Euler characteristics cannot be generalized to left-overwards. Moreover, we set up a four-dimensional analog of Yeung's norm inequality, which yields existential results for incompressible surfaces in three-manifolds and side-essential disks. These results extend to hypocompressible planes and sides-essential disks.

The orientation of light emitted from a laser is typically assumed to be randomly distributed, however achieving directional emission without external help or structure has been a difficult task.  We recently discovered that random light emission can be replaced with fully directional emission using only entropy as a guiding force in a laser setup without any specific structure.  Our results show that directional emission can occur in both incoherent and coherent regimes, as well as in complex systems with non-reversible light emission.  This discovery opens up new possibilities for controlling the behavior of lasers.

One of the key characteristics that distinguishes a cryptocurrency as a viable medium of exchange is its cost stability. This study develops a theoretical framework based on a decentralized, random-walk model of a distributed ledger, where the probability of exchange costs decreasing is proportional to the probability of transactions being added to the ledger. Using this model, we find that exchange costs follow a negatively skewed distribution with a cost stability property, where the variance decays at a rate of $1/k$ as the number of exchanges increases. This model accurately explains the observed, cost distributions of major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin and Ethereum.

We utilize an inverse scattering method to solve the feeble noise equation associated with the KP interface. The KP equation is solved through a transformation, reducing the problem to the inverse scattering of the Zakhar-Shabat system under specific boundary conditions. Our approach involves analyzing the boundary conditions at infinity to determine the time-dependent solution. The analysis uses the time evolution of the scattering coefficients, which are directly calculable from the feeble noise equation. The use of the time-evolution equations for the scattering coefficients allows us to validate and verify the results.

The discovery of the existence of compressive turbulence at sub-ion scales has been challenging due to its limited observational data. We have identified a significant event that allows us to analyze compressive magnetic and plasma structure in the solar wind at sub-ion scales. Using the Multi-Spacecraft technique from MMS, we found turbulent characteristics in compressive structures at scales ranging from 128 to 2048 kilometers. The analysis revealed a cascade of helical and polarized fields from large to small scales, ranging from 10 to 100 kilometers. The calculation of the kinetic energy transfer rate, based on the three-dimensional structure, indicated an energy transfer from larger scales to smaller scales at sub-ion scales, contradicting simulations that suggest an energy transfer from smaller scales to larger scales.

Our research explores the potential of generating attosecond pulses using synchrotron and free-electron laser sources within the extreme ultraviolet to soft X-ray spectrum. An altered technique has emerged, enabling the creation of such pulses via the direct interaction of intense lasers with highly-charged ions produced from laser plasma sources at next-generation FEL facilities. As a result, we anticipate the generation of attosecond pulses from the European X-ray Free-Electron Laser (XXFEL) and Extreme Ultraviolet Hard XUV (HHVL) lasers, given their expected output in the future. To facilitate this, our investigation focuses on the characteristics of these pulses, with an emphasis their application, particularly their utility, particularly their potential for use, particularly their anydynamics, electronic structure and interactions of matter at these energies.

Nonparallel shear flows are utilized as a reference for analyzing shear flows and other complex fluid dynamics systems. The choice of shear flow as a reference significantly influences the accuracy of the final results. The goal of this study is to extend the physical optics estimation (POE) method, combining features of several shear flow models and treating nonparallel effects as perturbations. The assumptions behind the models are evaluated to facilitate their practical application. By employing the Ostrovsky transform, the linear stability equations are simplified and converted into Helmholtz equations. The models are derived using properties of Bessel functions and involve calculations of Stokes' integrals. The derivation of the POE equations incorporates corrections based on Bessel functions. Four different models are examined: the viscous Couette flow, the Poiseuille flow, the Blasius boundary layer, and the Eckert shear flow. For each model, the corresponding POE equations are calculated. The results are validated using direct numerical simulation (DNS) for two types of waves: internal and edge. Specifically, the accuracy of the POE method is evaluated by comparing its predictions to those of the DNS across various scenarios, including variations in wave frequency, amplitude, and phase. The analysis reveals that the choice of shear flow model and treatment of nonparallel effects are crucial factors in the accurate prediction of wave behavior in shear flows.

Evaluating the extent of partisan manipulation in election maps remains a pressing challenge in related research. Recent developments in parties' strategic maps aim to reduce the influence of partisan manipulation while maintaining map quality. This paper introduces Simulated Heating, a novel method allowing researchers to quantify the impact of partisan manipulation on maps. By incorporating maps into a closure system with inherent structural constraints, Simulated Heating generates a series of progressively modified versions of the original map. These iterations start with the original map and continue through increasingly distorted simulations until the resulting maps significantly deviate from the initial framework. This process enables the analysis of how maps evolve under different levels of distortion. We apply Simulated Heating to maps representing maps released after and prior to the 2020 U.S. presidential election to illustrate how the method tracks changes in various factors as maps become significantly altered. Furthermore, we explore the potential of using Simulated Heating to assess the reliability of maps by examining the stability of classified outcomes across different levels of distortion.

The detection of patterns in images is crucial for quality control in the industry. However, variations in patterned images pose challenges for defect identification. In this research, an innovative method combining GHOG and matrix completion is introduced for identifying flaws on textured textile surfaces. The method leverages the GHOG feature to normalize patterned images, enhancing defect detection. Furthermore, an in-depth study of textiles reveals that most units adhere to a consistent structure, enabling the use of the matrix completion technique to pinpoint anomalies. The matrix completion is applied to the difference image between a reference and the target image, yielding improved defect recognition. Experimental results on three textile images demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed technique, outperforming comparable methods.

Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have led to the development of more intelligent navigation systems. However, these systems often struggle due to several limitations, including: 1) the lack of a standardized method for comparing different navigation policies during training, 2) difficulties in generalizing navigation policies when environments change, and 3) the reduced sample efficiency of RL methods. To overcome these challenges, we have modified a variational information maximization framework to evaluate the exploratory potential of navigation policies. By incorporating a self-supervised approach that doesn't rely on labeled data, we can compare policies at different stages of training and thereby improve sample efficiency. Furthermore, to enhance policy generalization, we have integrated a new framework that allows the system to adapt to new EVs without needing to retrain from scratch. Our approach successfully overcomes these challenges and demonstrates better performance than existing methods in navigation.

This study establishes a minimum limit on the rate at black holes gain or lose mass due to interactions with other black holes or as they move through a gaseous environment. This bondi mass reduction rate is crucial in understanding how black holes evolve. We establish a minimum rate by examining interactions between two black holes and also by analyzing the decrease in mass as a black hole moves through a gas. This minimum rate will serve as a parameter in a proposed model for simulating black hole populations, known as the field of mass-segregation agentless black hole population dynamics.

The initial stars formed within massive galaxies around 100 million years after the Big Bang. These early stars might have assembled in clusters at the heart of these galaxies, potentially leaving behind clusters of black holes long after the first stars had disappeared. In the coming decade, more sensitive gravitational wave detectors will be able to spot these black hole clusters. Studying these objects could provide valuable insights into the early universe, including insights into the first stars and their galaxies. This paper investigates how these black hole clusters evolve within clusters in galaxies that formed around the heart of the first stars. Using computer simulations, researchers tracked the gravitational wave signals from these clusters over the first 100 million years. They discovered that the black hole clusters emit a significant number of gravitational waves, which could be easily detected by future detectors. They estimated that the most active clusters will be able to be detected up to 300 to 400 megaparsecs away, based on the brightness of galaxies where these clusters are found. They identified particular black hole mergers that could be easily detected up to 30 megaparsecs away, which could be used as a starting point for further studies into the early signals.

This paper details our approach to detecting incidents in power distribution networks using data-driven methodologies. An algorithm is presented that leverages data to identify incidents by analyzing anomalies in substation voltage readings, automatically determining base patterns and detecting deviations. Critical parameters for incident identification, such as timeframes and threshold variations, are established. The effectiveness of our methodology is demonstrated through simulation using the MARPSO model.

We define specific categories associated with quadratic forms using generators and relations. It's proven that these categories have a unique, invariant characteristic, essentially because they have four homogeneous generators. This allows us to identify them as arising from projective spaces with quadratic surfaces. Additionally, our study provides new insights into the structure of the derived category of vector bundles on a quadric surface.

Text-based games offer a perfect platform for researching text comprehension. TextWorldExpress, a simplified version of TextWorld, enables large-scale simulation using graphics, allowing for the comparison of different neural models by mimicking the performance of ideal agents. A recent advancement employs a memory-based neural model with joint image and text understanding, joint sampling, and recurrent learning, which produces surprisingly simple yet effective results. This model reaches over one million steps per second, matching the performance of human players. Furthermore, it exhibits strong capabilities in learning to use memory, which excels in playing tasks compared to other models, both internally and in broader tests. This model's architecture has potential applications in completing text-world tasks requiring sustained use of stored information. A preprint of this research is available at the ArXiv repository.

We develop a theoretical framework for understanding topological insulators devoid of spatial dependencies, specifically suited for models exhibiting geometric flaws. In our approach, we define the magnetic band gap as the minimum energy difference between occupied and unoccupied states. Under specific conditions, this concept gives rise to K-bundles exhibiting monodromy in relation to the magnetic band gap. Our formalism is validated through application to the Berghammer-Templin model, an 11D topological insulator model exhibiting monodromy associated with a flux introduced by Tohru Kawai.

This research introduces a novel spatial extreme value model aimed at addressing the challenge of predicting multivariate extreme events in the ocean. The model builds upon existing approaches by using a conditional extreme value model based on a bivariate extreme value distribution. The model's parameters are estimated using a novel approach that incorporates a novel measure of dependence on a compact domain. The model's applicability is demonstrated through a case study involving the prediction of the most extreme wind patterns over the North Sea during ocean storms, thereby identifying areas at highest risk for severe events.

Let $k$ be a $p$-adic field and $d$ an integer greater than one. The paper establishes the existence of a finite set, denoted $C(k,d)$, such that all rational functions $f$ from the non-Archimedean Green function to the complex numbers, definable over $k$ with degree greater than one, will assume only values in $k$ or within the set $C(k,d)$. Additionally, the paper proves that these functions are dependent on a finite number of base functions for each non-Archimedean field and any given exponent. A similar result is achieved for Archimedean green functions and constant on a non-Archimedean ring. These findings serve as rational dynamics counterparts to the Minkowski theorem and the strong Liouville theorem.

Robots' working limits are often constrained by their design, requiring task completion within a reduced version of their full potential, known as a reduced operability domain (OD). Expanding this domain improves task efficiency but demands task switching mechanisms to navigate within and outside the restricted domain. Directly translating human movements from the reduced to the full domain assumes task consistency, but this isn't guaranteed in practice. Instead, we've developed an innovative task-consistency-agnostic method using time-series matching, projecting key pose keypoint distances via iterative closest point (ICP) optimization. This approach refines ICP's standard performance by considering the manifold of poses and ensuring smooth projections through manifold learning. Experimental validation on 30 subjects demonstrates the effectiveness of this method in teaching robots new tasks within a expanded domain, with increased assessment success rates.

A current search for doubly suppressed Higgs boson pair production at the LHC using 80 TeV proton-proton collision data is in progress. In a proposed analysis using $\textrm{b}$-jets and leptonic $\textrm{W}$-boson decay products at the $\textrm{ATL}\textrm{A}$ and $\textrm{ATL}\textrm{A}$ experiments, the invariant mass of $\textrm{b}$-jets is focused on the region around two times the Higgs boson mass. The analysis uses the matrix element technique to distinguish signal from background, specifically using JIMMY for signal and RAPGAD as a background model. A cut-based analysis with 80 TeV, 300 fb$^{-1}$ (equivalent to $\textrm{LHC}\textrm{Z}$ at 14 TeV with 3000 fb$^{-1}$) and various $\textrm{p}_\textrm{T}$, $\texm{p}_\textrm{T}^{\texm{jet}}$, and missing transverse energy thresholds demonstrates the potential of this channel. In these scenarios, the matrix element technique significantly outperforms the $\textrm{b}$-jet only approach in both signal and background classification.

Our approach involves training networks to understand the 3D positions of rotating objects in simple scenes, using a self-supervised technique that's similar to address the problem of vanishing units in sequence learning. This technique leverages the temporal relationships between adjacent frames to create an accurate 3D representation of the object's rotation. As the camera and the object rotate, the training data is created without labels and rotates in 360 degrees, enabling the learning of 3D representations. This learning is then validated with real-world data from rotating objects, including letters and animals, and the results show improved performance in rotating and the accuracy of 3D representations also compares favorably to other methods.

In recent years, the spread of misinformation on social media has become a pressing concern, with false vaccine-related information specifically targeting COVID-19 vaccines driving new conversations and spreading harmful notions among diverse user groups. On Twitter, users engage in complex discussions, adopting various attitudes towards misinformation based on their opinions and experiences, yet the current understanding of how to identify the acceptance or rejection of misinformation in these contexts remains limited. This study presents a novel task that aims to identify acceptance or rejection of misinformation in Twitter discussions regarding false COVID-19 vaccine information, and introduces a new dataset containing 4,833 tweets from 13,111 accounts. Results from the study demonstrate that tweeters exhibit distinct patterns when expressing attitudes towards misinformation, with notable differences in their vocabulary and usage of names and handles, and even when control topics are excluded, consistent differences remain. Experimental findings indicate that tweeters' opinions on misinformation are strongly correlated with those from the control topic set, and various deep learning models were tested on the new dataset, with RoBERTa emerging as the top performer, achieving accuracies of 64.0%, 74.4%, and 82.8% across three scenarios.

High-intensity transient events known as solitons can produce Isolated Attosecond Pulses when applied to rarefied gaseous targets. To enhance this process, a two-stage counter-propagating laser setup is utilized, where a primary, unmodulated laser initiates plasma and a secondary, modulated petawatt pulse interacts with it to create an attosecond pulse. We investigate the influence of the plasma field, which develops within the single-frequency modulated peak of the pulse, on the generation of attosecond radiation. By leveraging this plasma field, we increase our ability to control and replicate the process, even in the presence of plasma instabilities and imperfections in the laser source.

We've analyzed recent findings on companion candidates in several binary stars affected by common envelope evolution.
  Using updated evolutionary models and more accurate mass estimates, we recalculated the mass loss that occurred during the common envelope phase.
  Our results indicate that the mass loss estimates are significantly lower than previous assumptions.
  When combined with existing constraints on binary star formation, companions to stars like Algieba, Alnitak, and Bellatrix are highly unlikely.
  Additionally, possible companions to stars like Mirach and Caelum are excluded based on our mass loss estimates.
  Although a companion to Alexel is possible, the range of its mass values would need to be unusually broad.
  Essentially, binary star evolution has very few viable candidate systems left.

This research focuses on analyzing localized nonlinear Schrödinger equation solutions, given an initial data with finite energy and the equation is set outside of a convex obstacle with a smooth surface. We demonstrate the existence of a definitive upper limit for the L^2 norm of the initial data, denoted as B_0. When the initial data's L^2 norm falls below this B_0 threshold, we can confirm the existence of localized explosive solutions.值得注意的是, the localized explosive solutions we found are unique. In the case of a spherical convex obstacle, we can confirm that the localized explosive solutions we found are unique.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that bypasses traditional discretization methods by integrating physical laws into a neural network model with no predefined assumptions. Although PI-NNs do not rely on predefined definitions, an implicit structure can be formulated to calculate residuals at key points, reflecting the extent to which the computed solution fails to satisfy the governing equations. This property of PI-NNs allows for the creation of an algorithm where neural network parameters are optimized in response to calculated residuals. Notably, existing research has not addressed the issue of adaptively introducing new variables to refine the implicit structure while accounting for physics constraints. This paper presents an innovative strategy for adaptively creating new points on an arbitrary domain based on estimated errors. The proposed method analyzes the local error caused by insufficiently accurate implications at key points and introduces new points only in areas with high error. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on linear convection-diffusion and a problem on an arbitrary domain with an arbitrary boundary condition.

We develop a comprehensive simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs with 3D atomistic  ferroelectric models.  The code considers Larkin's effect, the reverse field dependence of dielectric constant, and dielectric breakdown in multi-domain ferroelectric FELS. The Larkin effect significantly impacts field distribution at the domain wall and leads to an unusual decrease in dielectric constant near the domain wall under an applied field that opposes the domain direction.  Furthermore, the  Larkin effect causes a significant decrease in total capacitance in multi-domain ferroelectric FELS, which significantly differs from their single-domain counterparts.  To address this issue, we have created a new model to accurately simulate multi-domain ferroelectric FELS, which considers various factors such as atomistic simulations, various field dependencies of dielectric constant, and various hysteresis loops.  To accurately simulate multi-domain ferroelectric FELS, our model employs various atomistic simulations at different locations within multi-domain ferroelectric FELS, which considers various factors such as dielectric constant, leakage current, and resistance.  The model was validated by comparing its results with those of single-domain ferroelectric FELS, hollow FeFETs, and experiments, which shows good agreement between our model and experimental data.
